title: Something that really bothers me with Taxi Driver

commenti.body:
This is true with a lot of Scorsese's films, obviously - Wolf of Wall Street is a really clear one. KotFM is interesting as an exception - you don't really like the villains.

I think Scorsese's thing is that he is a deeply moral person with a clear sense of right and wrong, and for that reason is interested in what makes people do evil things. So he portrays evil people in a sympathetic way, from their own perspective, because it's interesting. He doesn't go out of his way to say that they're evil, but it's the background assumption. So people without strong moral senses - notably, teenage boys on the internet - do watch the films and like the evil people. Scorsese challenges his viewers to come to terms with the fact that evil people are often sympathetic and likable, and because many people are stupid and/or vicious many people don't manage it.

That is true. But I feel the film is more challenging for people who are too ready to dismiss people like Travis Bickle, and less challenging for people who feel like him. And I always wonder if Scorsese could've complicated that without making Taxi Driver any less than what it is.

I mean he does try to murder a politician because of sexual jealousy over one of his employees. It's not difficult to draw a moral line there. You've got to have some degree of trust in your audience to draw  their own conclusions, and that means some people are going to draw wrong conclusions.

I'm wary of discussing films on the basis what someone in the online memesphere says. More likely than not, you're chafing at teenage edgelords who've found Taxi Driver via Joker. But I will say:

As problematic as it may be to glamorize Travis and identify with him without critical distance, I find it just as emotionally and intellectually lazy to dismiss him altogether as a dumbfuck racist villain. Travis is (like Jake La Motta or Madame Bovary) a challenge to your empathy. He's the epitome of existential loneliness, of an alienation that extends not only to other people, but to things, the environment, and ultimately to his own self. The ugliness of his instincts is not excused, but it is brought to the fore through his lack of meaningful connection to the outside world. Which is, if we examine ourselves honestly, part of the human condition. When we are truly alone, we will likely become prey to the worst in us.

That's the exercise of watching Taxi Driver: Accept and endure and try to understand the POV of a depressed man who insulates and further isolates himself from the world through misguided hate and strange reveries. To vilify him is missing the point just as much as to glamorize him. He's human, we're human, we're all shit unless we care about each other.
I agree with all of that. Very well said.

This is a good take but I'd also like to add that this compulsion of people to raises their noses at films that happen to represent or simply *pre*sent a case of someone or thing that is antithetical to themselves is not only pretentious but truly has no place in a forum discussing art. If one's concern is moral cleanliness, they shouldn't be inviting artistic works into their personal lives because it will invariably cause dissatisfaction.

Of course, OP has most likely watched something far worse than Tax Driver, but chose this simply because he saw something online he didn't like -- that's fine. But there is more obscene art that exists in the world that isn't parody nor sarcastic, but simply antithetical. And to call all of it "bad" is tantamount to juvenile delinquency.

I still don't see how that is challenging to the fundamental worldview that people who feel like Travis have. Murdering a (probably corrupt, asshole) politician who probably made society the way it is, the way Travis feels alienated from, is not a challenge to that worldview. In fact, it might even be a rallying call to action.

tbh I don't know the answer myself, and maybe there's no answer. I'm just curious if there is one.

amazing way to imagine things I never said and never thought. 

It's funny how you're saying I saw something else and came here attacking Taxi Driver, when you clearly saw something you don't like and came here to vent your frustrations at me.

Pure projection
 
> But there is more obscene art that exists in the world that isn't parody nor sarcastic, but simply antithetical. And to call all of it "bad" is tantamount to juvenile delinquency and intellectual loitering.

How is that supposed to be directed at anything I said? 

Grow up.

I’m not familiar with these online fans you’re discussing, but I rewatched Taxi Driver recently and was thinking about this… in addition to the excellent points raised here by other commenters, I think one factor not to be overlooked is DeNiro himself in the role. He’s just so damn charismatic. Repulsive, yes; disturbing, yes… but I think there’s just something appealing about him that draws us in & makes us want to have empathy for Travis. If they’d used another actor, someone more grating or unlikable, the effect on the viewer might have been totally different, lacking that ambiguity which helps make the film so powerful.

The politician isn't portrayed as corrupt, unless I'm misremembering. All we know about him is he's a bland conservative. I don't think Scorsese has any obligation to step in and say "by the way, murdering politicians is wrong, folks!" It's something the film could have done if that's what he was interested in, but it isn't a flaw in the film.

I'll be more clear. It is more challenging for a well off person whose life is going great to watch this movie and get to like and sympathize with someone like Bickle.

It is less challenging for a person like Bickle to watch this film and get to hate the way which Bickle is responding to his feelings of loneliness and alienation. 

Maybe I'm stating something too obvious and thus you're trying to get at what I could be implying, but I'm not implying anything.

I'll say that even if the movie literally stops and has another character come and tell us that what Travis is doing is wrong then it still is not challenging the worldview at question.

I understand your viewpoint and I agree with it. but you're not getting at me, and I don't know what I could say more to fix that.
Yeah I think in that case we agree about what the film is doing. I just don't think it's a problem.

lol God help you OP 

Because you’re 100% right about the visual depiction of Travis’s racism, via the “time freezing” effect you describe (great way of putting it) among others, but holy shit you’d have to pay me by the minute to ever bother discussing it with people online. The vast majority (if not all) of people that might read and engage with your post, still wouldn’t dare to honestly check such moments in the film even if you fed them timestamps. Your post has barely taken off, and much of the response is already embarrassingl

But yes, it’s there, and I’m not surprised Scorsese and others confirm it. It was quite the “!” of realization when it clicked on my 2nd or 3rd watch, I believe it was specifically the time-freeze instance where Travis walks out the diner with Wiz to try to open up to him, and before they talk, there’s this extended glare he gives this group of Black teens(?) walking past

Best of luck to you lml

thanks! 

I think people have trouble discussing this without thinking it's only coming from a PC woke moralist angle, but that's incredibly bad faith. Like can we actually have nuanced conversations about art, you know, the thing woke and anti-woke people pretend they want?

Or they feel that I'm attacking the profound artistic quality that Taxi Driver reaches by bringing it down to discuss things like racism. But I feel it is through being specific about things like racism that Scorsese is actually able to go beyond and discuss something universal like alienation and existential loneliness. And ignoring it and not engaging with it to me means you actually don't appreciate Taxi Driver fully.

This is inherent in any film tracking a morally questionable character. I don’t see how this can be avoided by a director. Oliver Stone’s Wall Street inspired many to want to be stock brokers, I’ve see unironic posts of people aspiring to be like Patrick Bateman. You can only present your story in the best way you know and let people interpret it how they interpret it.

People who argue Travis isn't racist don't understand racism. Or, more charitably, they don't understand how Travis expresses his racism.


In the same way those people might find sympathy for a weirdo who takes his date to a porno, they might have never actively thought about how Travis's behavior toward others is gross and disgusting _and racist_.


I can understand their getting defensive if they haven't yet realized how that form of racism operates. They thought they were watching a movie about how a loner rose above his weirdo, creepy behavior and made something out of his life. Learning that _even this_ was yet another layer of ridicule is going to be a tough pill to swallow.

Thank you for saying what I’m getting at. Their reaction to Travis’s inner monologue of “here’s someone that stand ups to the filth. Here’s someone that said no.” is a triumphant celebration and affirmation of values, not a sad devolution into a state of violent psychosis. Schrader even sees Travis as being into Iris, and not totally doing what he did out of pure altruism.
